newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka rupee seen dipping seven percent over '97.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka rupee seen dipping seven percent over '97.

text.p: The Sri Lanka rupee should ease by about seven percent during 1997 as part of a gradual depreciation in the relatively stable currency, a Reuters poll of foreign exchange dealers showed on Monday.
The poll of eight foreign and local commercial banks showed that most expected the rupee to end 1997 at 60.85 for every dollar, against 56.70 at the start of 1997 and 58.48 on Monday.

But the current exchange rate was considered reasonable, the dealers said. A sharp slide was not expected due to Sri Lanka's economic conditions, such as a high budget deficit and heavy dependence on imports.
The assumption that the rupee would fall to about 60.85 was based on average annual depreciation of between five and eight percent in the past few years.
"The Sri Lanka rupee has depreciated about seven percent in the past several years, except in 1995 when the market saw an aberration of eight percent," said Standard Chartered Bank.
The individual forecasts for the year-end exchange rate varied from a high of 62.50 rupees to a low of 60 rupees.
The banks polled were ABN Amro Bank, American Express Bank, Bank of Ceylon, Deutsche Bank, Hongkong Bank, Hatton National Bank, Standard Chartered Bank and Seylan Bank.
Five of the eight banks said the present exchange rate was reasonable, given the country's economic priorities.
Seylan Bank, however, differed. "The right value is 60 rupees to the dollar to give exporters a competitive advantage", it said.
Most dealers also said the rupee could be considered stable since it did not fluctuate wildly over the long-term.

"Even so-called 'stable' currencies can have wild movements in the short-term. Going by this definition, the rupee is a stable currency since its movements are orderly in the long-term," ABN Amro said.

Hongkong Bank said it believed the rupee was stable since it traded well within the range quoted by the Central Bank. "There have been very few occasions where the market has put pressure on the Central Bank's trading range."
The Central Bank sets the dollar-rupee exchange rate range daily, taking into consideration inflation differentials between Sri Lanka and its trading partners and local demand and supply.

Deutsche Bank, however, said the rupee was not stable because "despite the buying and selling rates fixed by the Central Bank, the market on most occasions is unable to withstand heavy demand and supply".
All the dealers who were polled said the Central Bank should intervene in the market to maintain a stable exchange rate.
"At present, our budget deficit, which is approximately eight percent of GDP (gross domestic product), does not facilitate a free float of the rupee," said Standard Chartered Bank.
The state-owned Bank of Ceylon said the Central Bank should intervene since the rupee was not fully convertible and the exchange rate was mostly driven by local supply and demand.
The Central Bank's present system of quoting a two percent range and leaving the market to trade within that band was desirable, said Hongkong Bank.
"The Central Bank should not intervene directly in the market as long as the dollar trades within its band," it said.
